blocks.text: Start with what the evidence can and cannot tell you. I could not find a study that measures how video editors split their day between cutting, admin, email and typing. Any page that gives a single percentage for editors is guessing, and this one is no exception. What you can do is read the job description, look at the wider office data, then log your own week.
Where an editor's day goes, and what the numbers do not say

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics describes the job as screen work. It says nearly all editing is done on a computer. Editors are often trained in one specific editing program. They also look at every frame to decide what to keep or cut. That is close attention, and nobody else can do it for you.

The BLS counts 39,400 film and video editing jobs in 2025. About 35% of those editors are self-employed, and 31% work in motion picture and video industries. If you are self-employed, the scheduling, invoices and client email are yours too. Nobody in a studio will handle them for you.

The wider office data is broader. Microsoft's Work Trend Index looked at commercial knowledge workers in a 28-day window ending March 2023. It found 57% of their time went to communication, such as meetings, email and chat. The other 43% went to creating documents, spreadsheets and presentations. Email alone took 15% of time.

Those are not editors, so treat the numbers as a rough guide. Here is a worked example. If email takes 15% of a 40 hour week, that is 6 hours of inbox time. Microsoft found the top quarter of email users spend 8.8 hours a week on email. Your own inbox could sit anywhere on that range.

Attention is the third piece. Gloria Mark's research finds people average 47 seconds on any one screen before they switch. That number measures screen time, not focus, and her page does not give a median. Still, a timeline, a browser and a chat window can mean many switches in one hour. Each switch is a chance to lose your place in the cut.

Try a simple log before you buy anything. For one normal workday, write down each app you open and the time you leave the timeline. Mark the switches that were admin rather than edit decisions. Your own log is more useful than any average, including the ones on this page.
Which AI tools for video editors help with which part of the day

Think of AI tools for video editors in three groups. Some type for you. Some look things up. Some sit beside the software and answer questions about what is on screen. Pick the group that matches the time you lose, not the tool with the longest feature list.

items: Dictation: speak notes, client replies and log lines, and have the text land at your cursor. In Lazur, hold fn.
Screen help: ask what a control does or where a menu item lives, and hear the answer. In Lazur, hold ⌥ ⌘.
Research: send a question to run in the background and get back a summary and a report.
Drafting: ask for a first draft of a client reply or a delivery note, then edit it before you send.
Everyday tasks: timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, notes, music, and opening apps and links.

blocks.text: Lazur covers all five groups above. It does not edit footage, click buttons in your editor or file things for you. Lazur points, explains and guides. You still make every cut and every click. Plan your day with that limit in mind, because it changes what you can hand off.
Finding footage and exports in Finder without losing your place

Most editors lose a few minutes a day to files. You know the cut exists, but not which folder it went into. Finder has quick fixes for that. Press ⌘ 2 to switch a window to list view, so dates and sizes sit in columns. Press ⌘ ⇧ G to type a folder path. Use Finder > Go > Recents to see what you opened last.

Lazur helps when the path is not in your head. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask, 'Where is the export folder for the Client Spring project?' Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. It does not open the folder or move anything. You decide what happens next.

If footage lives across several drives, the [Finder guide for video editors](/for/video-editors/finder) covers the layout in more detail. Keep one naming rule for the whole team. Name each export with the project, the version and the date, so a search can find it.
Mac requirements for Final Cut Pro, DaVinci Resolve and Premiere Pro

Before you add any AI tool, check that your Mac can run the editor you already use. The requirements differ for each app, and the sources I found disagree in places. Treat the vendor's own page as the final word. Write down the version and the date you checked.

Apple's Final Cut Pro tech specs list macOS 15.6 or later. They ask for 8GB of memory, with 16GB recommended, and 6.5GB of free disk space. Apple also says some features need macOS Sequoia and a Mac with Apple silicon. Other sources gave older or newer macOS minimums, so check the App Store listing before you upgrade.

Blackmagic Design lists DaVinci Resolve 21 and DaVinci Resolve Studio 21 on its tech specs page. That page does not state a macOS, chip or RAM requirement for Resolve itself. It points to the reference manual and support pages instead. It lists Mac 14.3 Sonoma or later for the Replay Editor peripheral, and it says the Fairlight Audio Accelerator is for Intel Macs only.

I could not open Adobe's Premiere Pro requirement pages, so I cannot give you a verified macOS minimum for Premiere Pro. Open Adobe's system requirements page yourself before you upgrade your Mac or your editor.

Dictating notes, client replies and log lines at the cursor

Dictation fits the admin that interrupts an edit. Hold fn in any app, speak, and let go. Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor. That works in Mail, Slack, Google Docs in Chrome, or a notes file. Dictation is included with Lazur. It is not the headline feature, so use it for the small writing you do all day.

Snippets help with text you repeat. Make one for your delivery spec, your invoice terms or your shot log line. Add names and terms that Lazur misses to your personal dictionary. Clipboard slots keep the text you need twice, such as a client's reference number.

Here is a worked example. You finish a rough cut and need to tell the director what changed. Hold fn and say rough cut two is in the review folder, scene four audio needs a pass, and color is still rough in the second act. Read the text before you send it. Any dictation tool can mishear a name.
Using research and drafts for the work that follows the cut

After the cut comes the paperwork. You check license terms, delivery specs and a client's deadline. You read release notes when your editor updates. These tasks pull you away from the timeline for longer than they should. Lazur can run them as research in its own Chrome tabs, then return a summary and a report.

A good research question names the version, the platform and the outcome you need. 'What changed in the latest DaVinci Resolve release about audio?' beats 'Tell me about Resolve.' Read the report before you act on it. Vendors change menus between versions, and I did not check recent release notes for this page.

Drafting works the same way. Ask for a first draft of a reply that says the color pass needs two days. Then add the facts only you know, such as your rate, the revision count and the date. Lazur does not know your contract or your client history unless you say so in the request. For browser-based editing tools, see [Chrome for video editors](/for/video-editors/chrome).
Everyday tasks and what Lazur keeps on your Mac

Lazur covers the small jobs too. It sets timers, adds Apple Reminders, makes Calendar events, writes notes, controls music and volume, opens apps and links, searches the web and runs Shortcuts. Ask the way you would ask a colleague. 'Remind me to send the invoice at 4 pm' is one sentence, and the reminder lands in Apple Reminders.

Lazur keeps memory of what you asked and did. That memory is kept on your Mac. It helps when you ask, 'What did I say about the audio on scene four?' Know what it keeps before you rely on it for client work.
Privacy: what Lazur sees and where your data goes

Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. When you ask, the audio and a screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. Those are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. That is what Lazur says about how it handles your data, so read it before you install.

This matters for footage. Unreleased cuts, client faces and NDA material can all show up on screen. Before you hold the shortcut over a client project, check your contract and the rules your employer sets. Those rules come first, not any product page.
Mistakes people make with AI tools in a video edit

items: Asking the tool to make the cut. Lazur points and guides, and you still make every edit decision.
Trusting a shortcut from an old tutorial. Menus change between versions, so check the help for the version you run.
Sending confidential footage into a chat without checking your client contract first.
Upgrading macOS before you check that your editor supports it.
Judging a tool on one slow afternoon. Track a normal week, then decide.

blocks.text: Another mistake is treating a demo as proof. I found no independent data on how much time these tools save editors, so this page makes no such claim. Measure your own week with the log described above, and keep only the habits that stick.

faq.question: Do AI tools for video editors cut the footage for me?
faq.answer: Not with Lazur. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It points at things on screen, explains them out loud, guides you one click at a time, and drafts or types text. Check each editor's own help for any built-in AI features, since those come from the app maker.

faq.question: Does Lazur work inside Final Cut Pro, DaVinci Resolve and Premiere Pro?
faq.answer: Lazur works with any app you have open, because it sees your screen while you hold ⌥ ⌘. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. Check each editor's requirements separately.

faq.question: What Mac do I need for Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. Your editor has its own requirements, so check those too.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. The audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Can I dictate client email with Lazur?
faq.answer: You can dictate into any app with fn. Before you send confidential client material through any AI tool, check your contract and the rules your employer sets. Those rules come first.

faq.question: Is there a free way to try Lazur?
faq.answer: There is a free trial, and no credit card is needed. It starts when you first open the app. Current plan terms are on the pricing page.

faq.question: Why does this page not give time percentages for editors?
faq.answer: I found no study that measures how editors split their day. The Microsoft figures cover all commercial knowledge workers, using March 2023 data, so they are a rough guide only.

faq.question: Are shortcuts from older tutorials still right?
faq.answer: Often not. Menus change between app versions. I did not check recent release notes for these editors, so use the app's own help for the version you run.

faq.question: Does Lazur keep a record of what I asked?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur keeps memory of what you asked and did, and that memory stays on your Mac. Know what it keeps before you rely on it for client work.
